newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - China spends big to secure oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - China spends big to secure oil.

text.p: China decisively shifted the global balance of world oil to the East on Wednesday in a bold move to secure much needed oil supplies into the next century.
In two seperate deals the China National Petroleum Company (CNPC) agreed to spend more than $5 billion in Kazakhstan and Iraq in return for oil to meet its burgeoning demand.
"This is to gain access to secure supply," said Mehdi Varzi, oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London. "I would say the Chinese links with the Gulf area will strengten over the next ten years."
Western and Eastern oil companies have been battling in recent years over the rights to oil in the turbulent Middle East Gulf and former Soviet central Asia.
On Wednesday Kazakhstan announced a $4-billion oil deal with CNPC including an ambitious plan for a pipeline to its eastern neighbour China.
In a separate move CNPC on Wednesday also signed a $1.2 billion deal to develop the one-billion barrel Ahdab oil field in the south of Iraq.

CNPC has promised to invest $4 billion in the Kazakh Aktyubinsk oil enterprise over the next 20 years, with $585 million to be invested from 1998 to 2003, in return for a 60 percent share in the company.

Aktyubinsk is located in western Kazakhstan and has estimated oil reserves of 483 million tonnes. CNPC vice president Wu Yaowen said current annual output of crude of 2.2 million tonnes (44,000 barrels per day) would double by 2000.
CNPC's plan to build a 3,000 km (2,000 mile) pipeline worth $3.5 billion to export the oil to the northwestern province of Xinjiang was the main reason Kazakhstan chose CNPC.
"There were some good offers from American firms," Eduard Utepov, head of the privatisation department at the Kazakh finance ministry, said in reference to tender losers Texaco Inc and Amoco Corp.
"But most interesting for us was the Chinese offer on oil transport," he said.
Last month Kazakhstan signed a huge deal to build a pipeline taking oil from massive reserves in the west of the country to Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossisk.
China also faced tough competition for the Iraqi deal.
Oil companies have already been scrambling to secure rights to develop Iraqi oil fields when United Nations sanctions imposed on Iraq after the Gulf War in 1991 are eventually lifted.
Over 50 foreign firms have been in contact with Baghdad, industry sources said.
With global oil demand tilting towards booming Asian economies the tussle to secure supplies in the next century is likely to hot up.

Kleinwort's Varzi saw Chinese oil demand growing anywhere between six and 10 percent in recent years while demand in the United States has recently been around two percent, according to the International Energy Agency.
China's need to secure oil supplies arises "directly out of a growing gap" between huge demand and more modest domestic production, said Varzi.
CNPC expects to import 30 million tonnes of crude oil this year compared to 22.6 million in 1996. But imports could rise to 40 million tonnes in 2000.
"The east is definitely going to drive the market," said Bob Finch, head trader at Vitol SA, the world's largest independent oil trading and refining company.
